title: Tuning single-molecule fluorescence by atomic-scale control of the local environment
authors: Thiago G. L. Brito, Daniel Arribas, Sofia Canola, Klaus Kuhnke, Tomáš Neuman, Anna Rosławska
abstract: Molecules that absorb and emit light play a central role in microscopy, light-emitting devices and photosynthesis. Their fluorescence arises from well-defined radiative transitions that are governed by the electronic states and their coupling to the nuclear motion that are influenced by the local environment. Yet the effect of controlled atomic-scale variations in the emitter surroundings remains unexplored. Here, we use scanning tunneling microscopy combined with optical spectroscopy to investigate the optical response of a single phthalocyanine to the change in the position of a nearby molecule, controlled with precision better than 100 pm. Upon decreasing the intermolecular distance, the molecular emission energy redshifts and its line profile evolves. Supported by theoretical calculations, we disentangle the electronic and nuclear contributions to the changes in fluorescence. We find that the redshift originates from the interaction between the excitations of the two molecules, while the lineshape changes reflect modifications of the molecular rotational degree of freedom and non-equilibrium dynamics. We extend this control to larger assemblies, where one molecule tunes the energies of two chromophores, mimicking the environmental tuning in photosynthetic systems. Our study provides atomic-scale insight into how the local environment affects the optical properties of molecular systems.
summary: The researchers demonstrate that single-molecule fluorescence can be tuned with picometer precision by physically manipulating the surrounding environment using STM. By combining spectroscopy with theoretical modeling, they disentangle how spectral shifts arise from electronic coupling while line shape changes reflect modifications to the molecule's rotational dynamics and energy dissipation pathways.
main_problem: The study investigates how precisely controlled, atomic-scale variations in the local molecular environment affect the fluorescence properties of single molecules.
main_result: Fluorescence emission energy can be tuned by several tens of meV through environmental control, and spectral line shapes reveal distinct contributions from electronic coupling and modifications to the molecule's rotational dynamics.
method: The research combines high-resolution optical spectroscopy with scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to physically manipulate the intermolecular distance between chromophores.
model_or_system: The system uses phthalocyanine molecules ($	ext{ZnPc}$) whose fluorescence is probed while interacting with a nearby molecule ($	ext{PtPc}$). Theoretical models, such as the quantum harmonic torsional oscillator model and TDDFT, are used to analyze spectral shifts and fine structure changes.
key_observables: Molecular emission energy (spectral redshift), line profile evolution (fine structure/libronic progressions), and angular displacement ($\Delta\phi$).
important_parameters: Intermolecular distance ($d$), controlled with precision better than $100 	ext{ pm}$; spectral shifts up to $\sim 15 	ext{ meV}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximating rotational potentials as parabolas and using remote resonant energy transfer (RET) excitation to minimize artifacts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the progressive redshift and change in peak shape of the $	ext{ZnPc}$ emission spectrum as the distance between molecules decreases, alongside detailed spectral fits showing evolution of libron populations and adsorption angles.
paper_structure: The paper systematically maps the optical response by varying the separation distance ($d$) using STM/spectroscopy. Analysis progresses from observing simple shifts to fitting complex line shapes using torsional oscillator models, culminating in understanding the physical origins (electronic vs. nuclear) of these changes in larger assemblies.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct experimental platform for studying environmental coupling effects on quantum emitters, bridging concepts from cavity QED and molecular physics by controlling the local potential landscape at sub-nanometer scales.
